sections.html: The Harlequin barb (Trigonostigma heteromorpha) is one of the most popular ornamental fish worldwide. Its beautiful colours and peaceful temperament make it an ideal inhabitant of a community tank.

• Family: Cyprinidae
  • Adult size: 4.5 cm (1.75 inches)
  • Life expectancy: 6 years
  • Social: Peaceful, suitable for a community aquarium
  • Tank level: Top to mid-dwelling
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (about 40 litres)
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Breeding: Egglayer
  • Care: Intermediate
  • pH: 6.0 to 7.5
  • Hardness: Up to 12 dGH
  • Temperature: 23 to 28°C (73 to 82°F)

Harlequin rasboras are ideal for smaller community aquariums and should be kept in schools of 8-10 to best show their shoaling behaviour.
The harlequin rasbora is native to Malaysia, Singapore, Sumatra, and southern Thailand.

It inhabits streams and waters characterized principally by their low mineral content and high concentrations of dissolved humic acids, which is typical of water that flows through swamped forests. The waterlogged soils of these forests inhibit the complete decay of leaf litter, resulting in the formation of peat, which leaches humic acids. These conditions resemble those found in the blackwater habitats of South America.

Rasboras are a true freshwater family of fish and are never seen in brackish waters. They prefer the lowland waters of southeastern Asia, where the water is soft and acidic. Harlequins prefer an environment with areas of dense vegetation, an open area for swimming, a dark substrate, and subdued lighting.

An aquarium intended to house harlequin rasboras should be planted with live plants. Create open areas for swimming between stands of plants such as Cryptocoryne species, which are among the plants that inhabit the harlequin rasbora's native waters.

• Temperature: 23 to 28°C (73 to 82°F)
  • pH: 6.0 to 7.5
  • Hardness: up to 12 dGH

Harlequins readily accept all foods but prefer live foods whenever possible. In nature, their diet consists primarily of insects. However, they will accept frozen foods, freeze-dried foods and flake foods. A varied diet will ensure that digestive problems or susceptibility to disease do not occur. Brine shrimp, daphnia, and any type of worm are excellent supplemental foods, particularly when conditioning before breeding.
Despite the coloration, the blue and golden sports show no difference to the wild form: they are beautiful and peaceful community fish that should always be kept in small schools.

The harlequin rasbora is a shoaling fish; it should be kept in schools of eight to 10 individuals. Schools of even larger numbers make for a beautiful display. You can keep harlequins with any fish as long as it is not large and predatory. It will not nip at or quarrel with any other species. Some potentially good tankmates may include cardinal tetras, one betta, neon tetras, small barbs, dwarf gouramis, danios, other small rasboras, and cory catfish.

It is a smaller fish, so keep it with like-sized specimens; larger fish might be attracted by its shimmer and try to make a meal out of it.

The Spruce Pets FAQ: up to 10 harlequin rasboras can generally be kept in a 20-gallon (about 75 litres) aquarium, depending on adult size, swimming behaviour and other tank inhabitants. They can generally coexist with a single betta. They are generally compatible with peaceful shrimp of similar size, though they may eat shrimp fry or smaller shrimp species.

Male harlequins are more slender and a bit smaller than females. Although they share similar colors and patterns, the males tend to be more brightly colored than the females. In addition, the distinctive black wedge covering the posterior of the fish may be more rounded in males and more angular in females.

It is hard to believe today that this species was once impossible to breed. In the 1930s breeders had to learn that water chemistry can be very important for the breeding of fish, and they learned it from the harlequin barb. Nowadays millions of these fish leave the breeding farms each year.

Harlequins are among the more difficult tropical freshwater species to breed, however, spawning may be achieved if you provide the proper conditions. Select young specimens and condition them with live foods such as daphnia and mosquito larvae before the spawning attempt. Unlike other popular rasboras, which are egg-scattering spawners, harlequin rasboras are egg layers.

You can breed groups of young harlequins in a single aquarium. When spawned in groups, keep two males for every female. Hobbyists who wish to simulate natural conditions as closely as possible may filter the aquarium water over peat to replicate the humic acid concentrations of the native waters, although this is not necessary if the basic water chemistry parameters (hardness no higher than 4 dGH, pH around 6.4) are correctly maintained. The optimum water temperatures for spawning are between 24 and 27°C (76 and 80°F). Add Cryptocorynes or similar broad-leafed plants to the breeding tank.

Once the breeding tank is prepared, introduce the breeding stock late in the day. Spawning usually begins in the morning and is initiated by the male dancing and trembling before the female. This behaviour is intended to direct the female beneath a suitable plant for depositing the eggs. The male may nudge the sides of the female and rub his belly against her back to move her to the spawning location.

When ready to spawn, the female turns upside down and rubs her belly against the underside of a leaf, signaling the male to join her. The male approaches her while continuing to tremble, then wraps himself around her body and fertilizes the eggs as they are released. Six to 12 eggs are laid at a time. The fertilized eggs rise and adhere to the underside of the leaves. During one to two hours, as many as 300 eggs may be laid, although 80 to 100 is more typical.

When spawning is complete, remove the breeding stock from the aquarium, as they will consume the fry once they hatch. At water temperatures of about 27°C (80°F), the eggs hatch in approximately 24 hours. The fry are translucent and remain attached to the leaf for another 12 to 24 hours, during which time the yolk sac is absorbed.

Once this is completed, the fry become free-swimming and require very fine foods such as live infusoria for seven to 14 days, after which they can feed on newly hatched brine shrimp. If infusoria are unavailable, commercially prepared fry foods for egglayers may also be used. Young harlequin rasboras reach sexual maturity in approximately six to nine months.

Over the years mutants appeared and were bred from then on. The two best known are the blue and the golden sports.

For wholesale customers: "Blue" has code 452523, "Gold" code 452563 on the Aquarium Glaser stocklist. Aquarium Glaser supplies the wholesale trade exclusively.

Text & photos: Frank Schäfer

Of the more than five dozen species of rasbora, the harlequin is arguably the most popular. Often referred to as a red rasbora, the body is a reddish-copper color accented by a striking black wedge covering the rear half of the body. The distinguishing triangular patch begins near the dorsal fin and comes to a point near the base of the caudal fin.

This species looks similar to the Pork Chop or Lamb Chop Rasbora (T. espei), the Narrow Wedge Rasbora (T. hengeli) and Somphong's Rasbora (T. somphongsi), and these species can be differentiated primarily by the size of the dark wedge. They are listed from largest to smallest triangular patch.
• Robert Woods. Harlequin rasbora care guide & species profile. Fishkeeping World.
